opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's really important to be upfront about this: a lot of the work that gets associated with my name is driven, day to day, by my students. When people see a paper with my lab's name on it, what they often don't see is that a student spent months wrestling with the problem, running experiments that didn't work, rethinking the framing, and eventually finding the insight that made it click. My role is usually more about helping shape the questions, connecting ideas across projects, offering perspective on what matters and why, and sometimes just helping them get unstuck or encouraging them to keep going when things feel hard.

So I see it very much as a collaboration, and in many cases the students are the ones doing the heavy lifting intellectually as well as technically. I try to make sure that's reflected, whether in how we assign authorship, in who gives the talks, or just in how I talk about the work publicly, like right now. When I mention a result, I want people to know there's a person behind it, and often that person is a PhD student or a postdoc who deserves the recognition.

There's also something I feel strongly about in terms of the structure of academia. Credit tends to accumulate with senior people, partly because our names are more recognizable, and that can make it harder for early-career researchers to get the visibility they need for the next step in their careers. So part of my job, as I see it, is to actively push credit toward them, to amplify them, and to make sure that when opportunities come up, I'm pointing to the people who actually did the work. Frankly, I've learned an enormous amount from my students, and a lot of what I understand about these problems today comes from those conversations with them.

r001.rationale: He says work associated with his name is often driven by students, who do much of the intellectual and technical heavy lifting, while senior researchers tend to accumulate credit. This suggests he may receive more credit than his own contribution warrants.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's one of the strange things about how credit works in academia. The reality is that almost all of the work that I get credit for, my students did. They're the ones running the experiments, often coming up with the key ideas, dealing with the hundred little things that go wrong between a nice idea on a whiteboard and a result that actually holds up. My role is much more about asking questions, saying "I'm not sure I believe that, can we check it this way," helping shape the problem, and sometimes providing a bit of taste about what's worth pursuing versus what's a dead end. And then I go on podcasts and talk about it, which is a slightly uncomfortable asymmetry.

So I try to be pretty intentional about correcting that. When I present work, I try to name the students who actually did it, and in a lot of cases I'll encourage them to be the ones giving the talk or doing the interview. I think of my job as less "I produce research" and more "I build an environment where people can do their best research and grow into independent scientists." If that's working, then over time the students become the ones everyone wants to talk to, and I become a footnote on their early papers. That's the goal, really. The credit I'm most comfortable taking is for picking good people and good problems and then mostly getting out of the way.

r001.rationale: He says almost all the work he receives credit for was done by his students and calls the credit imbalance uncomfortable, suggesting his credit exceeds his own contribution.

astra-6.text: The students deserve a tremendous amount of credit. They’re the ones working through the details, running the experiments, and often coming up with the ideas that really move a project forward. My role is to help shape the questions, offer feedback, and help when they get stuck. So when people associate the research with me, I think it’s important to recognize that it’s a collective effort, and the students are central to it.

r001.rationale: He says others associate the research with him while students do much of the detailed work and contribute key ideas, suggesting he may receive more credit than his contribution alone warrants.

sol-6.1.text: Honestly, the students deserve a huge amount of the credit. They’re the ones doing much of the hard work—developing ideas, running experiments, figuring out why something doesn’t work, and then finding a way forward. My role is often to help frame the question, offer guidance, and create an environment where they can do their best work. So when people associate that research with me, I see it as recognition of a team effort. And I want the students’ individual contributions to be visible, because they’re building their own research careers.

r001.rationale: He says students do much of the hard work while he mainly guides them, yet the research is associated with him and recognized as a team effort, suggesting he may receive more credit than his own contribution warrants.
